caption: Thurmaston National School, Main Street
history:
In 1844 Thurmaston's National School opened, built for the sum of £600 on land donated by Squire Thomas Allen. Weekly church or chapel writing lessons were replaced by a professional curriculum if people were able to afford the 2d fee.
The majority of village children were from poor framework knitting families so bad attendance was commonplace until the fee was abolished in 1891. An extra classroom wing was added in 1869, with separate staircases for boys and girls.
Dormer windows in the upper story and a further extension improved the school by the turn of the century when pupil numbers rapidly increased. By 1925, however, the building was in a poor state. Back yards containing the outside toilets, coalbunker and the air-raid shelters for WW2 had often flooded owing to the proximity of the River Soar. A rise in the school leaving age further added to the difficulties. The two chapels and the Memorial Hall were brought into use as extra classrooms. Roundhill Secondary Modern had drawn away the older children in 1929, but it was not until 1954 when Church Hill Road Infants took the younger ones that the situation eased. A Junior department addition to Church Hill and the opening of Eastfield C.P. School finally closed the doors on the old building to the children of Thurmaston in 1968. Used since as a Resources Centre the ‘Old School’ is currently used for church and community activities, it still stands proudly opposite St. Michael’s Church.
